Local models change the shape of the problem. A cloud service hides its cost behind a network request: you send audio or text, wait, and something comes back. On the Mac, the cost is visible. Memory fills with weights, the fans spin up during a long dictation, and the battery drains a little faster than you'd expect. In exchange you get privacy, offline use and no per-minute bill. Whether that trade is worth it depends less on benchmark scores than on how the app feels: how quickly words appear, whether the cleanup is trustworthy, and whether reading aloud starts promptly and keeps going without gaps. Those are the things this evaluation tries to measure, with recordings and passages that look like real use rather than clean audiobook speech. If the local models fall short, that's a useful answer too. It tells us where the gap is, how large it is, and what would have to change before trying again.
